source_refs.note: Exercise 12.2, Question 4: find c so that the limit at x = -1 exists (book p.234). Answer key PDF 310: c = -1.

blocks.prompt: 4 If \[f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 2, & x \le -1 \\ c + 2, & x > -1 \end{cases}\]find \(c\) so that \(\lim_{x \to -1} f(x)\) exists.
blocks.explanation:
A "find the constant" question: the limit at \(x = -1\) must exist.
A limit exists exactly when LHL = RHL, so we get one equation in \(c\).
Plan: find both one-sided limits in terms of \(c\), set them equal, solve.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x + 2\) for \(x \le -1\), \(c + 2\) for \(x > -1\).
To find: \(c\) such that \(\lim_{x \to -1} f(x)\) exists.
Method: The limit exists if and only if \(\lim_{x \to -1^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^+} f(x)\).

Left hand limit
\[\lim_{x \to -1^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^-} (x + 2)\]
\[= -1 + 2 = 1\]
Why: Left of \(-1\) the first piece is used.

Right hand limit
\[\lim_{x \to -1^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^+} (c + 2)\]
\[= c + 2\]
Why: Right of \(-1\) the function is the constant \(c + 2\) (it does not contain \(x\)), so its limit is itself.

Set them equal and solve
\[c + 2 = 1\]
\[c = 1 - 2 = -1\]
Why: Only this value makes the two one-sided limits equal.

Check
\[c = -1:\ c + 2 = 1\]
\[\text{LHL} = \text{RHL} = 1\]
Why: With \(c = -1\) both sides approach 1, so \(\lim_{x \to -1} f(x) = 1\) exists. (Here \(f(-1) = 1\) too, so \(f\) is even continuous there.)
